Choose headings by **rank**, not by visual size — the size is CSS's job. ### ARIA: a safety net, not a primary plan Native HTML (labels, headings, alt text, semantic elements) covers ~90% of accessibility. **ARIA** fills the gaps: `aria-label` names an element that has no visible text, and `aria-describedby` points to a longer description. ```html

The practical shortcut: use the right element, label everything, keep a logical order, and test with a keyboard and a screen reader. ### Skip links Keyboard users do not want to tab through every nav link on every page. codeSnippets.output: A semantic page skeleton: header, nav with skip link, main with a section, and footer.

exercise.instruction: Build a semantic page skeleton. In the <head>, add a meta description tag (meta name="description"). In the <body>, add a <header> with an h1, a <nav> with a link to #main, a <main> containing a <section> with an h2, and a <footer>.
hints: Hint 1: Add <meta name="description" content="..."> inside the head.
Hint 3: Put at least one <section> with an <h2> inside <main>.

quiz.question: Which element marks the one unique main content block of a page?
Why must headings never skip levels?
options: Because screen reader users navigate by heading outline and skipping destroys it
Because the browser refuses to render them
